annotations.annotation_text: Compound opening word indicating circularity and eternal return (Giambattista Vico's ricorso). Resumes the incomplete sentence closing the novel on page 628 ('A way a lone a last a loved a long the'). Also invokes the River Liffey flowing through Dublin, personified as Anna Livia Plurabelle (ALP).
sources: McHugh, Roland. Annotations to Finnegans Wake (4th ed.). https://jhupbooks.press.jhu.edu/title/annotations-finnegans-wake
Campbell, Joseph and Robinson, Henry Morton. A Skeleton Key to Finnegans Wake. https://archive.org/details/skeletonkeytofin00camp

annotations.annotation_text: Inversion of Adam and Eve, evoking original sin and human genesis while locating the reader precisely in Dublin: the popular name for the Church of the Immaculate Conception on Merchant's Quay near the Liffey.
sources: Tindall, William York. A Reader's Guide to Finnegans Wake. https://archive.org/details/readersguidetofi00tind
Dublin Historical Record: Adam and Eve's Church. https://www.jstor.org/stable/30104271

annotations.target_phrase: swerve of shore to bend of bay
annotations.annotation_text: Refers to the curved Dublin coastline from Howth Head around Dublin Bay and Sutton isthmus to Dalkey, tracing the geographical embrace of the bay where the Liffey enters the Irish Sea.
sources: Norris, David and Flint, Carl. Joyce for Beginners. https://archive.org/details/joyceforbeginner0000norr

annotations.annotation_text: The mid-sentence lowercase opening thrusts the reader in media res into an eternal stream of consciousness. It connects etymologically to French 'rêverons' (let us dream together) and links with the book's final words 'a long the' to form a never-ending circle.
sources: Wikipedia: Finnegans Wake. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Finnegans_Wake
Scholarly analyses of Wakean circularity. https://fweet.org/

annotations.annotation_text: Joyce's inversion of 'Adam and Eve' to 'Eve and Adam's' restores primacy to Eve, subverting the patriarchal narrative. This structural reversal establishes the text's pervasive pattern of reversed and cyclical causality.
sources: Finnegans Web. http://finnegansweb.com/wiki/index.php/Page_3

annotations.annotation_text: Multilingual pun fusing the Roman Emperor Commodus, English 'commodious' (spacious/convenient), Latin 'vicus' (lane, street, village), and Giambattista Vico (1668–1744), the Italian philosopher whose cycle of history (divine, heroic, human, ricorso) provides the scaffolding for Finnegans Wake.
sources: Vico, Giambattista. Scienza Nuova (The New Science, 1725). https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/vico/
Ellmann, Richard. James Joyce. https://archive.org/details/jamesjoyce0000ellm

annotations.annotation_text: Acronym HCE, establishing the universal everyman protagonist Humphrey Chimpden Earwicker. Geographically, Howth Castle situated on the peninsula guarding the northern entrance to Dublin Bay.
sources: Glasheen, Adaline. Third Census of Finnegans Wake. https://archive.org/details/thirdcensusoffin0000glas
Howth Castle Estate History. https://howthcastle.ie/history/

annotations.annotation_text: 'Commodius' carries a double meaning, denoting both spatial capacity (commodious) and the scatological (commode). Together, the phrase signals that the narrative follows Giambattista Vico's cyclical pattern of rise, fall, and resurrection.
sources: Scholarly search results on Viconian cycles. https://fweet.org/

annotations.annotation_text: This phrase contains the first occurrence of the protagonist's initials, H.C.E. Howth Head is mythologically identified with the head of sleeping giant Finn MacCool, while Howth Castle is a real medieval estate inhabited by the St. Lawrence family.
sources: Wikipedia: Howth Castle. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Howth_Castle
Scholarly sources on Finn MacCool. https://fweet.org/

annotations.annotation_text: Evokes Sir Tristram of Lyonesse from Arthurian legend and Wagner's opera Tristan und Isolde. "violer d'amores" puns on viol d'amour (instrument) and viola d'amore / violator of love (viol/rape). Tristram was born in Armorica (Brittany).
sources: Bédier, Joseph. The Romance of Tristan and Iseult. https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/14244
Wagner, Richard. Tristan und Isolde Libretto. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tristan_und_Isolde

annotations.annotation_text: French "pas encore" (not yet) fused with "rearrived". Announces the pre-historical mythical timeframe where actions have both not yet occurred and are perpetually repeating in Viconian ricorso.
sources: Beckett, Samuel, et al. Our Exagmination Round His Factification for Incaminasion of Work in Progress. https://archive.org/details/ourexagminationr0000unse

annotations.annotation_text: Armorica was the ancient Celtic name for Brittany (Northwestern France), from where Tristram hailed. Fuses with "North America" to foreshadow the transatlantic migration of Irish descendants.
sources: Caesar, Julius. Commentarii de Bello Gallico. https://www.thelatinlibrary.com/caesar/gall.html

annotations.annotation_text: Geographical and bodily metaphor: refers to Ireland as a jagged protrusion off Europe, the Sutton isthmus connecting Howth to the Dublin mainland, and phallic/anatomical topography.
sources: O'Hehir, Brendan. A Gaelic Lexicon for Finnegans Wake. https://archive.org/details/gaeliclexiconfor0000oheh

annotations.annotation_text: Triple pun: the Peninsular War (1807–1814) fought by the Duke of Wellington, the "peninsular" isolation of Howth and Ireland, and Tristram's sexual / phallic conquest ("penis-isolate").
sources: Wellington, Arthur Wellesley, 1st Duke of. Dispatches. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arthur_Wellesley,_1st_Duke_of_Wellington

annotations.target_phrase: topsawyer's rocks by the stream Oconee
annotations.annotation_text: Allusion to Mark Twain (Samuel Clemens) and Tom Sawyer. The Oconee River flows through Laurens County and the city of Dublin, Georgia, founded by Peter Sawyer, an immigrant from Dublin, Ireland.
sources: Twain, Mark. The Adventures of Tom Sawyer. https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/74
New Georgia Encyclopedia: Dublin, Georgia. https://www.georgiaencyclopedia.org/articles/counties-cities-neighborhoods/dublin/

annotations.annotation_text: Laurens County, Georgia (containing Dublin, GA). "gorgios" is Romani (Gypsy) slang for non-Gypsies / gentiles, contrasting with the indigenous and wandering tribes.
sources: Borrow, George. Romano Lavo-Lil: Word-Book of the Romany. https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/2951

annotations.annotation_text: Pun on Dublin, doubling numbers, and "mumper" (an old cant/slang term for a beggar or vagabond; also mumbling). Highlights the proliferation of duplicate Dublins across the globe.
sources: Grose, Francis. 1811 Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue. https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/5402

annotations.target_phrase: avoice from afire bellowsed mishe mishe to tauftauf thuartpeatrick
annotations.annotation_text: Synthesizes God's voice from the burning bush to Moses (Exodus 3:2) with Saint Patrick. "Mishe mishe" is Irish "Mise, mise" ("I am, I am"); "tauftauf" is German "taufen" (to baptize); "thuartpeatrick" blends "Thou art Peter" (Matthew 16:18: Tu es Petrus) with Patrick.
sources: The Confession of Saint Patrick. https://www.confessio.ie/etexts/confessio_english#
Vulgate Latin Bible: Exodus 3 and Matthew 16. https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Matthew+16%3A18&version=VULGATE

annotations.annotation_text: Fuses "very soon after", venison (the hunted deer; Jacob's deception of Isaac with savory venison), and "venison" / "Venus" (erotic pursuit and fertility).
sources: Genesis 27 (Jacob and Esau with Isaac's venison). https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Genesis+27&version=KJV

annotations.target_phrase: kidscad buttended a bland old isaac
annotations.annotation_text: Allusion to the biblical patriarch Isaac in Genesis 27, deceived by his cad son Jacob (wearing goatskin kid) who supplanted Esau. Also echoes Parnell ("the Chief"), Charles Stewart Parnell's betrayal, and elder generations displaced by youth.
sources: Frazer, Sir James George. Folk-Lore in the Old Testament. https://archive.org/details/folkloreinoldtes01frazuoft

annotations.annotation_text: Blends the proverb "all's fair in love and war" with Jonathan Swift's Esther Vanhomrigh ("Vanessa"), whose tortured romantic triangle with Swift and Esther Johnson ("Stella") mirrors the two warring temptresses of the Wake (Issy and her mirror).
sources: Swift, Jonathan. Cadenus and Vanessa (1726). https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cadenus_and_Vanessa
Ehrenpreis, Irvin. Swift: The Man, His Works, and the Age. https://archive.org/details/swiftmanhisworks01ehre

annotations.target_phrase: sosie sesthers wroth with twone nathandjoe
annotations.annotation_text: French "sosie" (double/twin/lookalike) + sisters: Stella and Vanessa wrathful with Jonathan Swift ("twone" = two + one; "nathandjoe" = Nathan + Joe / Jonathan Swift). Also evokes Swift's Tale of a Tub.
sources: Swift, Jonathan. A Tale of a Tub (1704). https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/4737

annotations.target_phrase: Rot a peck of pa's malt had Jhem or Shen brewed
annotations.annotation_text: Parody of "This is the House That Jack Built" ("This is the malt that lay in the house that Jack built"). Introduces the twin sons Shem the Penman and Shaun the Post ("Jhem or Shen"), Jameson and Guinness malt brews, and the sins of the father.
sources: Opie, Iona and Peter. The Oxford Dictionary of Nursery Rhymes. https://archive.org/details/oxforddictionary0000unse_m4u1
History of Guinness Brewery at St. James's Gate. https://www.guinness-storehouse.com/en/our-story

annotations.target_phrase: arclight and rory end to the regginbrow
annotations.annotation_text: Electric arc lighting combined with "rory" (Irish "ruadh", red, or Latin "ros/roris", dew/dawn), aurora, and Rory O'Conor (last High King of Ireland). "regginbrow" is inverted German "Regenbogen" (rainbow), signalling God's covenant with Noah after the deluge.
sources: Genesis 9:13 (The Covenant of the Rainbow). https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Genesis+9%3A13&version=KJV
MacKillop, James. Dictionary of Celtic Mythology: Rory O'Conor. https://www.oxfordreference.com/view/10.1093/acref/9780198609674.001.0001/acref-9780198609674-e-2727

annotations.annotation_text: The circular rainbow reflecting upon the primordial waters of the deep (Genesis 1:2: "and the Spirit of God moved upon the face of the waters"). German "Wasserfläche" (water surface) and Latin "aqua".
sources: Hayman, David. The 'Wake' in Transit. https://archive.org/details/wakeintransit0000haym

annotations.annotation_text: Capitalized cosmogonic Fall: Lucifer's fall from heaven, Adam and Eve's fall in Eden, Humpty Dumpty's fall from the wall, Tim Finnegan's fall from the ladder in the ballad, and Wall Street's stock crash of 1929.
sources: Atherton, James S. The Books at the Wake. https://archive.org/details/booksatwake0000athe

annotations.annotation_text: First of the ten 100-letter thunderclaps (this opening one has 101 letters). In Vico's philosophy, thunder is the terrifying voice of God that drives primitive humanity into caves to establish language, religion, and marriage. Fuses words for thunder from 10 languages: Hindi, Arabic, Greek, Japanese, French, Italian, Irish, Swedish, Danish, English.
sources: Vico, Giambattista. The New Science (The Thunder and the Giant Age). https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/vico/
Bishop, John. Joyce's Book of the Dark. https://archive.org/details/joycesbookofdark0000bish

annotations.annotation_text: Etymological breakdown: 'bababadal' (Tower of Babel), 'gharaghta' (Hindi/Arabic), 'kamminar' (Japanese), 'ronnkonn' (General Cambronne's Waterloo 'Merde!'), 'bronn' (Greek), 'tonnerron' (French), 'tuonn' (Italian), 'thunn' (English), 'trovarr' (Portuguese), 'hounawnskawn' (Swedish/Irish), 'toohoohoordenen' (Danish), 'thurnuk' (Irish). Originally fewer letters, Joyce added 'babab' to hit the symbolic 100-letter total.
sources: Finnegans Web. http://finnegansweb.com/wiki/index.php/Page_3
Stack Exchange Literature. https://literature.stackexchange.com/

annotations.target_phrase: once wallstrait oldparr is retaled early in bed
annotations.annotation_text: Conflates Wall Street financial collapse (1929) with Thomas Parr ("Old Parr"), an English centenarian said to have lived to 152 years; also echoes Humpty Dumpty who sat on a wall, and bedtime stories / wake gossip.
sources: Dictionary of National Biography: Thomas Parr. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Tom_Parr

annotations.annotation_text: Refers to John Keble's popular devotional poetry collection "The Christian Year" (1827) and traditional minstrel songs, ballads, and wandering street bards chronicling the human condition.
sources: Keble, John. The Christian Year. https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/15440

annotations.target_phrase: The great fall of the offwall entailed at such short notice
annotations.annotation_text: Connects Humpty Dumpty with feudal legal property "entail" and the suddenness of catastrophic downfall in both cosmic and comic registers.
sources: Blackstone, Sir William. Commentaries on the Laws of England (On Estates in Tail). https://avalon.law.yale.edu/subject_menus/blackstone.asp

annotations.target_phrase: pftjschute of Finnegan, erse solid man
annotations.annotation_text: The comic sound effect of falling ("pftj") and "chute" (French chute: fall/descent). Tim Finnegan of the Irish-American comic street ballad "Finnegan's Wake" who fell from a ladder drunk, and "erse solid man" (Irish solid man; also Earth / ear / solid citizen).
sources: The Ballad of Tim Finnegan's Wake (Traditional Irish-American Street Ballad). https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Finnegan%27s_Wake
O'Lochlainn, Colm. Irish Street Ballads. https://archive.org/details/irishstreetballa0000oloc

annotations.target_phrase: humptyhillhead of humself prumptly sends an unquiring one well to the west
annotations.annotation_text: Humpty Dumpty blended with Howth Hill (the giant HCE's head in the Dublin landscape, lying with head at Howth in the east and feet to the west in the Phoenix Park). Promptly / inquisitorially looking westward.
sources: Kenner, Hugh. Dublin's Joyce. https://archive.org/details/dublinsjoyce0000kenn

annotations.annotation_text: The recumbent giant's upturned toes pointing up at Castleknock in Phoenix Park, marking the western extremity of the dormant titan's recumbent body.
sources: McHugh, Roland. The Sigla of Finnegans Wake. https://archive.org/details/siglaoffinnegans0000mchu

annotations.target_phrase: knock out in the park where oranges have been laid to rust
annotations.annotation_text: Knockmaroon Gate and Castleknock in Phoenix Park. "Oranges" refers to King William III (William of Orange) and the Orangemen of the Battle of the Boyne (1690), contrasted with the Irish Green ("rust upon the green").
sources: Curtis, Edmund. A History of Ireland. https://archive.org/details/historyofireland0000curt

annotations.annotation_text: Origin of love and Dublin: Dublin's first (devil's first) love for the River Liffey (Anna Livia Plurabelle, "livvy"). Conflates Dublin foundation, Adam and Eve, Lucifer, and the eternal romance of landscape and river.
sources: Hart, Clive. Structure and Motif in Finnegans Wake. https://archive.org/details/structuremotifin0000hart
